items.prose: $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{A}^T$ projects onto the column space of a 4 × 2 matrix $\mathbf{A}$ with independent columns.
items.question: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.why: $\mathbf{P}$ sends every vector perpendicular to $C(\mathbf{A})$ to $\mathbf{0}$, so it cannot be undone.
Cancelling needs $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$, and a 4 × 2 matrix has none.

feedback.correct: Projections are symmetric and idempotent, and so is $\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each statement on a vector perpendicular to $C(\mathbf{A})$.

explain.text: Projecting twice is projecting once, so $\mathbf{P}^2 = \mathbf{P}$, and $\mathbf{P}^T = \mathbf{P}$ from the formula. Expanding gives $(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P})^2 = \mathbf{I} - 2\mathbf{P} + \mathbf{P}^2 = \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P}$. $\mathbf{P}$ kills the perpendicular space, so it has no inverse.

items.prose: Two columns of a design matrix are almost the same signal: their correlation is 0.9999. You fit by least squares.
items.question: Why prefer QR to solving $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{b}$?

options.text: Forming $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ squares the condition number, so rounding can wipe out the difference between the columns

options.why: In exact arithmetic both give the same $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$. The difference is how much rounding error creeps in.
QR costs about twice as much as forming $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$. It is chosen for accuracy, not speed.
With independent columns it is invertible, just badly conditioned here.

feedback.correct: QR works with $\mathbf{R}$, whose condition number equals that of $\mathbf{A}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what happens to a small difference when you form $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$.

explain.text: Nearly dependent columns give $\mathbf{A}$ a large condition number $\kappa$. $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ has $\kappa^2$, so twice as many digits are at risk. QR solves $\mathbf{R}\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{b}$, and $\mathbf{R}$ keeps $\kappa$.
